summary: Describes an extensibility mechanism for Kerberos V5 when used over TCP. It uses the reserved high bit in the length field to negotiate TCP-specific extensions. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A secret flag on a message's length lets two sides agree on extra features.

questions: kerberos kdc tcp length high bit
what is the kerberos tcp extension mechanism
what does the high bit in the kerberos length field mean
how does a kdc negotiate extensions
subtitle: A way for Kerberos clients and servers to negotiate extensions over TCP using a spare bit in the length field.

tldr.problem: Kerberos V5 over TCP starts each message with a length field whose high bit was reserved for future expansion, but nothing said what to do when that bit is set.
tldr.mechanism: When the high bit is set, the other 31 bits of the first 4 octets form an extension bitmask. The client sends a request or a PROBE and the KDC answers with zero if it supports the extensions, or with the set it does support.
tldr.outcome: It gives TCP-specific Kerberos extensions a common negotiation step and a new IANA registry. The unprotected length field allows downgrade attacks, so clients and KDCs should enforce a policy.

today: RFC 5021 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4120, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: A Reserved Bit Gets a Meaning
sections.content:
The Kerberos V5 specification (RFC 4120), in section 7.2.2, reserves the high-order bit in the initial length field for the TCP transport for future expansion. RFC 5021 updates RFC 4120 to describe what happens when that bit is set. The mechanism is meant for extensions that are specific to the TCP transport.

Clients are not forced to use it; they are expected to use it only when they want to negotiate a particular extension.
sections.plainLanguage: The message length had one spare switch nobody used. This RFC says what flipping it means.

sections.title: The Extension Bitmask and PROBE
sections.content:
When the reserved high bit of the request length field is set, the remaining 31 bits of the initial 4 octets are read as a bitmap, the extension bitmask. Each bit can request one particular extension. Other documents are expected to define the details for particular bits.

A 4-octet value with only the high bit set, so the bitmask is all zeros, is called a PROBE. A client may send a probe to learn which extensions a KDC supports, or it may set particular bits directly if it does not need to ask first.
sections.plainLanguage: Each of 31 little switches stands for one feature. Flip a switch to ask for that feature. Flip none to just ask what is on offer.

sections.title: The Exchange
sections.content:
The client MUST begin by sending a 4-octet value with the high bit set, either a PROBE or a request for specific extensions, and MUST NOT send more data until the server responds.

If the KDC supports the requested set, it MUST reply with a 4-octet zero value, 0x00000000, and MAY send additional data right after, as the negotiated extension specifies. A zero value cannot be confused with a normal reply, because a conforming RFC 4120 implementation never sends one: a KRB-ERROR is always of non-zero size.

If the KDC receives a PROBE, or does not support every requested bit, it MUST return 4 octets with the high bit set and the bitmask showing what it does support. It then MUST wait, and the client MUST send a second 4-octet value with the high bit set. If that second value is a PROBE or an unsupported extension, the KDC MUST close the connection; this lets a client shut down when a required extension is missing. If it is a supported extension, the KDC replies with the zero value as before.

Both sides SHOULD wait for the other to respond and SHOULD NOT close the connection prematurely, though resource considerations may limit how long they wait.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask, the server either says okay or shows what it can do, and you pick again. If it cannot do what you need, you hang up.

sections.title: Rules for Servers and Extensions
sections.content:
A KDC MUST NOT support the extension mechanism if it supports no extensions. In that case it MUST return a KRB-ERROR with KRB_ERR_FIELD_TOOLONG and MUST close the TCP stream, just as an implementation that does not understand the mechanism would.

If a request sets more than one bit and the extensions do not say how they interact, the KDC MUST treat it as a PROBE or unsupported extension. Each extension MUST describe the structure of protocol data after the length field and the behaviour of client and KDC; it may be a protocol with its own message framing. An extension that reserves multiple bits MUST describe how they interact.
sections.plainLanguage: A server with no special features acts as if it never heard of the switches. Anyone who adds a feature must explain exactly how it works.

sections.title: Interoperability Problems
sections.content:
Implementations with TCP support that do not conform to RFC 4120 may mishandle the high bit. A KDC might close the TCP connection without any response and log an error. When the RFC was written, this problem existed in modern versions of popular KDC implementations.

A client that gets no sensible answer might assume the KDC lacks the mechanism and remember that semi-permanently, taking care to avoid surprising the user when the KDC is later upgraded. Implementations might also allow enabling or disabling the mechanism per realm. The RFC leaves these compatibility details unspecified.
sections.plainLanguage: Some old servers do not know about the spare switch and just hang up. Clients may remember that and not ask again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The initial length field is not protected. An active attacker who can modify traffic between client and KDC could make the client think the server lacks this mechanism, a downgrade attack, or interfere with which extensions are agreed, which can also downgrade.

The RFC offers two mitigations: a policy in clients and the KDC to reject connections lacking the desired properties, and having the negotiated extension send a cryptographic checksum of the offered extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone in the middle could scribble over the mark and trick you into using the plain version. Rules about what you will accept, or a check over what was offered, stop that.

sections.title: The Kerberos TCP Extensions Registry
sections.content:
IANA created a registry called "Kerberos TCP Extensions". Bits 0 to 29 are available for registration, and bit 30 is reserved by RFC 5021. Values 0 to 29 are registered after IESG Approval; assigning value 30 requires a Standards Action that updates or obsoletes this document.

The IESG acts as steward of the namespace, considering whether a registration is justified given its limited size and confirming it is not harmful to the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list of which switch means which feature. Most switches are free, and one is kept back.
